title: Origins of Pharmacognosy
summary: How humans turned plants, fungi and animals into medicines, from ancient remedies to the first purified drugs.

lessons.title: What Is Pharmacognosy? From Crude Drugs to Pure Compounds

levels.kid:
Long before there were pharmacies, people found medicines in nature. They chewed willow bark for aches. They used the bark of the cinchona tree to fight a fever called malaria. A dried leaf, root or bark used as medicine is called a **crude drug**.

But nature is tricky. One leaf might be strong and the next one weak. That made old plant medicines hard to trust.

**Pharmacognosy** (say: far-mak-OG-no-see) is the science of medicines and poisons that come from plants, fungi, animals and the sea. Pharmacognosists are like detectives. First they check that a plant is really the right one. Then they find the special healing chemical inside and pull it out pure. A pure medicine works the same way each time.
levels.hs:
**Pharmacognosy** is the study of medicines and toxins from natural sources: plants, fungi, bacteria, animals and sea creatures. The name joins two Greek words: **pharmakon** (drug, and also poison) and **gnosis** (knowledge). It first appeared in German writing in the early 1800s. J. A. Schmidt used it in 1811, and C. A. Seydler put it in the title of an 1815 work, Analectica Pharmacognostica.

For most of history, medicine meant **crude drugs**. These are natural materials that are collected, dried and sometimes powdered, such as leaves, roots, bark, seeds, resins or latex. Crude drugs have two big problems:
- **Variable strength.** The amount of active chemical changes with the plant variety, soil, climate, harvest time and storage.
- **Mistaken identity.** One dried root can look like a different, sometimes toxic, root.

The breakthrough came when chemists learned to isolate the single **active compound**. Example: cinchona bark from South America had treated malarial fevers for centuries. In 1820 the French pharmacists Pierre-Joseph Pelletier and Joseph-Bienaimé Caventou isolated **quinine** from it. Pure quinine could be weighed exactly, so every batch had the same strength.

Most of these useful chemicals are **secondary metabolites**. A plant does not need them for basic growth but makes them for defense and signaling, such as bitter alkaloids that deter hungry animals. Pharmacognosy still matters today: roughly a third of approved small-molecule drugs are natural products or derived from them.
levels.college:
Pharmacognosy began as a descriptive science, identifying crude drugs by their appearance, and became a chemical one. Modern definitions (for example, the American Society of Pharmacognosy's) cover the physical, chemical, biochemical and biological properties of drugs and potential drugs of natural origin, plus the search for new ones.

**Kinds of crude drugs**
- **Organized** drugs have cellular structure: leaves (senna, digitalis), bark (cinchona), roots and rhizomes (ginger), seeds and flowers.
- **Unorganized** drugs lack cells: gums (acacia), resins, latex (opium is the dried latex of unripe Papaver somniferum capsules), and fixed or volatile oils.
Pharmacopoeias name them in Latin by species and part, such as Digitalis purpureae folium (purple foxglove leaf).

**Quality control of a crude drug** asks three questions:
- **Identity**: macroscopic features, microscopy (stomata, hairs called trichomes, calcium oxalate crystals) and chromatographic fingerprints such as thin-layer chromatography (TLC).
- **Purity**: limits on foreign matter, ash, moisture, pesticides, heavy metals and microbes.
- **Content (assay)**: how much active compound is present, or a **marker compound** measured as a quality indicator even if it is not proven to cause the effect.

**Why purification transformed medicine**
Crude drugs are mixtures whose composition shifts with genetics (chemotypes), environment, harvest and drying. Before chemical assays existed, digitalis leaf was standardized by **biological assay**: measuring its effect in animals. Isolating the active principle solved this. A crystalline compound has a defined structure, purity and potency. The early 1800s produced a cascade of isolations: morphine from opium (about 1804 to 1817), then strychnine, quinine (1820) and caffeine. Pure compounds also let scientists study mechanisms and structure-activity relationships, and later make semisynthetic and synthetic analogues.

**The continuum today**
Medicines span a spectrum: crude herb, then extract (tincture or dry extract), standardized extract, isolated pure compound, semisynthetic derivative, and finally a synthetic drug modeled on a natural scaffold. Pharmacognosy covers the whole range.
levels.phd:
The conceptual core of pharmacognosy is the distinction between **primary metabolism** (shared pathways of growth and energy) and **secondary metabolism**, a split articulated by Albrecht Kossel in 1891. Gottfried Fraenkel's 1959 paper on the raison d'être of secondary plant substances argued that these compounds evolved mainly as defenses against herbivores, especially insects. This ecological framing explains why so many are potent ligands for animal receptors, ion channels and enzymes: they were selected to disrupt animal physiology. The major biosynthetic families (alkaloids, terpenoids, phenylpropanoids and polyketides) also underpin **chemotaxonomy**, where chemistry tracks phylogeny and guides the search for related producers.

The quantitative problem with crude drugs is severe. Active constituents often make up well under 1% of dry weight, and content varies with:
- **Chemotype**: genetically distinct races of one species, such as thymol, linalool and geraniol chemotypes of Thymus vulgaris.
- **Induction**: jasmonate signaling after wounding or attack can raise defensive metabolite levels.
- **Post-harvest processing**: drying temperature, enzymatic degradation and storage.

Before analytical chemistry could resolve closely related cardiac glycosides, digitalis preparations were standardized biologically, for example by the Hatcher-Brody cat assay (1910) and pigeon assays, and expressed in reference units. Biological standardization measured integrated activity but was imprecise and ethically costly; chromatography and later HPLC displaced it.

The European Pharmacopoeia now classifies herbal extracts into three types:
- **Standardized extracts**: adjusted to a defined content of constituents with known therapeutic activity (senna sennosides).
- **Quantified extracts**: adjusted to a defined range of constituents not accepted as solely responsible for the effect (ginkgo flavonoids and terpene lactones).
- **Other extracts**: defined by production process alone.

The field's significance is documented in Newman and Cragg's serial reviews: across approvals from 1981 to 2019, roughly a third of small-molecule drugs were unaltered natural products, botanicals or natural-product derivatives, with a larger share if synthetic mimics of natural pharmacophores are counted.

A live controversy is **reductionism versus synergy**. Advocates of whole extracts invoke multi-target pharmacology; skeptics note that rigorous synergy demonstrations (isobolographic analysis) are rare, and that the pure-compound model delivered reproducibility.
levels.expert:
For a clinician-scientist, the crude-drug problem is not historical. It reappears whenever botanical material enters patients, research pipelines or supply chains.

**Identity failures have killed.** In early-1990s Belgium, a slimming preparation meant to contain Stephania tetrandra was made with Aristolochia fangchi, a confusion aided by the shared Chinese name fang ji. Aristolochic acid caused rapidly progressive interstitial nephropathy, many patients needed dialysis or transplantation, and urothelial cancers followed. The lesson: an assay of content does not confirm botanical identity. A product can pass a marker test if the marker was added, or occurs in the substitute.

**Authentication is multimodal.** DNA barcoding drew attention after Newmaster and colleagues (2013) reported widespread substitution in North American herbal products, and New York's attorney general acted on barcoding results in 2015. Critics pointed out that solvent extraction degrades DNA, so a negative barcode in an extract does not prove adulteration. Current practice pairs orthogonal methods: HPTLC fingerprints, LC-MS or NMR metabolomic profiles, and genetic testing on raw material.

**Crude versus pure in clinical decisions.** WHO advises against non-pharmaceutical Artemisia annua preparations, such as teas, for malaria. Artemisinin content is variable and often low, and subtherapeutic exposure risks treatment failure and selection of resistant parasites. This is the nineteenth-century argument for isolation, restated in modern antimicrobial terms.

**Supply as a research problem.** When the active compound is scarce, purification alone is not enough. Paclitaxel moved from Taxus brevifolia bark to semisynthesis from needle-derived precursors and then plant cell culture. Semisynthetic artemisinin from engineered yeast (Paddon et al., 2013) proved feasible but struggled economically against agricultural supply.

**Discovery pitfalls.** Without early **dereplication** (LC-MS and database matching to recognize known compounds), groups repeatedly rediscover familiar metabolites. Access and benefit-sharing obligations under the Nagoya Protocol (in force since 2014) now shape collecting, so legal provenance matters as much as chemistry.

**Open questions** include locating plant biosynthetic gene clusters, reconstituting long pathways in microbes (benzylisoquinoline alkaloid pathways in yeast, Galanie et al., 2015), and testing synergy claims with designs strong enough to separate genuine interaction from additive effects.

lessons.title: Ancient Pharmacopeias: Ebers Papyrus, Dioscorides and the Shennong Bencao

levels.kid:
Long, long ago, there were no drugstores. People used plants, honey and even animal parts to feel better. Clever healers wrote down which ones worked. These books were like recipe books for medicine.

- In Egypt, about 3,500 years ago, a long scroll called the **Ebers Papyrus** listed hundreds of remedies, like honey and garlic.
- In the Roman world, a Greek doctor named **Dioscorides** wrote about 600 plants. People copied his book for 1,500 years!
- In China, a book named after Shennong, the 'Divine Farmer', sorted 365 medicines into gentle ones and strong, risky ones. Legend says Shennong tasted plants himself to test them.

Some of these old remedies really worked. Scientists today still read these books for clues to new medicines.
levels.hs:
A **pharmacopeia** is an official book that lists medicines and explains how to identify and prepare them. The word comes from Greek *pharmakon* (drug) and *poiein* (to make). Long before modern chemistry, three ancient texts did this job and shaped medicine for centuries.

- **Ebers Papyrus** (Egypt, about 1550 BCE): a scroll roughly 20 meters long with around 700 remedies, mixed with magical spells. Ingredients included honey, garlic, castor oil, myrrh and aloe. Putting honey on wounds really helps, because honey is antibacterial.
- **De Materia Medica** by **Pedanius Dioscorides** (a Greek physician in the Roman Empire, about 50-70 CE): five books describing about 600 plants plus animal and mineral drugs. For each, he gave where it grows, how to prepare it and what it treats. It stayed the main drug reference in Europe and the Middle East for about 1,500 years.
- **Shennong Bencao Jing** (China, compiled around the 1st-2nd century CE): 365 drugs sorted into three grades, from safe 'upper' tonics to toxic 'lower' drugs used only to treat disease. It is named after Shennong, the legendary 'Divine Farmer' said to have tasted herbs.

Here is one real example of an ancient drug that worked. The Shennong text lists **ma huang** (*Ephedra*). In 1885, the Japanese chemist Nagai Nagayoshi isolated its active compound, **ephedrine**, which raises blood pressure and opens airways. Pharmacognosy often follows this path, from an old herbal record to a pure chemical.
levels.college:
Strictly speaking, these ancient works are **materia medica** (descriptions of medicinal substances) rather than pharmacopeias in the modern sense of legally binding official standards. Still, they share the core functions: identify the source, describe preparation, and state uses and dangers.

**Egypt.** The **Ebers Papyrus**, written in hieratic script around 1550 BCE and probably copied from older sources, was acquired by Georg Ebers in 1873 and is held in Leipzig. It contains roughly 700 formulas for problems from intestinal worms to eye disease, mixing rational remedies with incantations. Drugs came from plants (castor, garlic, juniper, frankincense), animals (honey, fat, even dung, the so-called 'filth pharmacy') and minerals (copper salts, natron). The roughly contemporary **Edwin Smith Papyrus** is a surgical text of 48 trauma cases, mostly of the head and spine. It holds the earliest known written descriptions of the brain's surface, the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid.

**Greco-Roman world.** Dioscorides, from Anazarbus in Cilicia, travelled widely, possibly as a Roman army physician. He rejected alphabetical order and grouped drugs by their properties. Entries give names and synonyms, habitat, appearance, preparation, uses and warnings. He described **opium** (from Greek *opos*, 'juice') collected from poppy capsules and warned of its dangers. He also described **mandrake** wine given before cutting or cautery to make patients insensible to pain. Mandrake contains the **tropane alkaloids** scopolamine and hyoscyamine.

**China.** The original Shennong Bencao Jing is lost. It was reconstructed from Tao Hongjing's annotated edition (around 500 CE), which expanded the list to 730 drugs. The core 365 drugs (252 plant, 67 animal, 46 mineral) fall into three grades:
- **Upper (120)**: nontoxic, 'nourish life', suitable for long-term use
- **Middle (120)**: strengthen the body; some are toxic
- **Lower (125)**: toxic, used to treat specific disease, not for prolonged use

This three-tier scheme is one of the earliest explicit attempts to rank drugs by toxicity.
levels.phd:
Reading these texts critically means separating three layers: the date of the surviving manuscript, the date of the content it preserves, and the identity of the substances it names.

**Dating and transmission.** The Ebers Papyrus is dated to about 1550 BCE because a calendar note on its back refers to year 9 of Amenhotep I, but its language suggests it copies earlier compilations. The Shennong Bencao Jing survives only through quotation. Tao Hongjing (456-536 CE) merged it with later notes, marking original entries in red ink and additions in black, and later scholars rebuilt the core 365 entries from such works. Dioscorides survives in many manuscripts, most famously the illustrated **Vienna Dioscorides**, made around 512 CE for the Byzantine noblewoman Anicia Juliana. It was translated into Arabic in 9th-century Baghdad (by Istifan ibn Basil, revised by Hunayn ibn Ishaq), fed Islamic pharmacy, and returned to Europe in Latin. Renaissance commentators such as Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1544) were still annotating it.

**The identification problem.** Ancient names rarely map cleanly onto Linnaean species. An Ebers remedy for a crying child uses *shepen*, often translated as poppy. That identification is contested, so claims of very early Egyptian opium use remain uncertain.

**Organizing principles.** Dioscorides criticized predecessors such as Crateuas and Sextius Niger and claimed firsthand observation. His grouping by 'affinities' of drug action is an early pharmacological classification. The Shennong preface links its three grades to roles in a formula (monarch, minister, assistant and envoy). It gives each drug a nature (cold, hot, warm, cool) and a flavor. It also lists seven relations between combined drugs, including mutual reinforcement and mutual antagonism, an early theory of drug interaction. Its central logic is that the tolerable duration of use shrinks as toxicity rises. This trade-off anticipates modern benefit-risk thinking.

**From materia medica to pharmacopeia.** Galen (2nd century CE) built on Dioscorides and lent his name to **galenicals**, crude-drug preparations. The first state-commissioned pharmacopeia was arguably China's Xinxiu Bencao (659 CE, roughly 850 drugs). Europe followed with the Florentine Nuovo Receptario (1498) and Valerius Cordus's Dispensatorium (Nuremberg, 1546).
levels.expert:
For a clinician-scientist, ancient materia medica are best treated as hypothesis generators: leads that are cheap to mine but expensive to validate.

**Leads that held up.**
- Changshan (*Dichroa febrifuga*), a Shennong fever drug, yields **febrifugine**. Its derivative **halofuginone** inhibits prolyl-tRNA synthetase (Keller and colleagues, 2012), a target now explored for malaria, fibrosis and autoimmunity.
- Castor oil, an Ebers laxative, works through **ricinoleic acid**, which activates the prostaglandin **EP3 receptor** on intestinal and uterine smooth muscle (Tunaru and colleagues, 2012). That mechanism was found roughly 3,500 years after the first recorded use.
- The 'AncientBiotics' project (Harrison and colleagues, 2015) recreated a 10th-century Anglo-Saxon eye salve of garlic, onion or leek, wine and ox bile. The mixture killed MRSA in wound-biofilm models, while single ingredients performed far worse.

**Pitfalls.**
- **Nomenclature hazards.** In the early 1990s, women attending a Belgian slimming clinic developed rapidly progressive kidney failure, and many later developed urothelial cancer. The Chinese name fang ji covered several plants, and *Stephania tetrandra* had been substituted with *Aristolochia fangchi*. **Aristolochic acid** forms DNA adducts that leave a characteristic A:T to T:A mutational signature, now used to trace exposure worldwide. Aristolochia species appear in classical herbals, including Dioscorides, where the name means 'best birth'.
- **Survival is not evidence.** Remedies persisted because copyists preserved authoritative texts, not because outcomes were tested. Placebo effects, natural recovery and regression to the mean all inflated apparent success.
- **Chemical variability.** Species, chemotype, harvest season and preparation all change composition. A recipe that 'worked' in antiquity does not guarantee a reproducible drug.

**Open questions.** Many plant identities remain unresolved, and the hit rate of text-guided screening compared with random screening is still debated. Ethics matter too: the Nagoya Protocol (in force since 2014) requires fair benefit-sharing when traditional knowledge leads to commercial products.

For neurosurgery, the lineage is direct. Dioscorides' mandrake and opium led to medieval soporific sponges and, eventually, to purified scopolamine and morphine.

lessons.title: Ethnobotany and Traditional Medicine Systems

levels.kid:
Long ago, there were no drugstores. People learned which plants could help them by watching, trying and remembering. Grandparents taught parents, and parents taught children, often through stories and songs.

In many places, special **healers** knew hundreds of plants: which leaf eased a tummy ache, which root calmed a fever, and which plant was poison.

Scientists called **ethnobotanists** visit these healers and listen carefully. Then chemists study the plants to find the helpful chemicals inside.

Here is a real story. Hunters in the Amazon rainforest made a dark paste called **curare** for their arrows. It made animals go floppy. Scientists studied it and made a medicine that helps surgeons keep muscles still during operations.

When a plant helps make a new medicine, it is fair to share the rewards with the people who taught us.
levels.hs:
**Ethnobotany** is the study of how people of a particular culture use the plants around them for food, tools, rituals and medicine. The word was coined by the American botanist **John Harshberger** in 1895. **Ethnopharmacology** is the closely related study of traditional medicines and how they actually work in the body.

The most famous ethnobotanist was **Richard Evans Schultes** of Harvard, often called the father of modern ethnobotany. He spent years living with Indigenous peoples in the Amazon and recorded the uses of thousands of plants.

Why does this matter for medicine? A plant used by many generations has already been through a kind of long-term human test. That makes it a smarter place to start looking than a random plant.

A real example: **curare**. Peoples of the Amazon basin made this arrow poison from vines such as *Chondrodendron tomentosum*. It paralyses muscles by blocking signals from nerves. In 1935 the chemist Harold King isolated its active compound, **tubocurarine**, which became one of the first muscle relaxants used in surgery.

There is also a fairness problem. When companies take traditional knowledge, patent it and profit without permission or payment, it is called **biopiracy**. International agreements now try to make sure the communities that share knowledge also share the benefits.
levels.college:
Traditional medicine is not one thing. It includes several organized systems, each with its own theory of the body, as well as countless local folk traditions.

**Major codified systems:**
- **Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM)**: health as balanced flow of **qi**, the interplay of **yin and yang**, and the **five phases**. It relies heavily on multi-herb formulas. Japan's **Kampo** is a standardized descendant.
- **Ayurveda** (India): health as balance of three **doshas**: **vata, pitta and kapha**. Treatments combine herbs, minerals, diet and lifestyle.
- **Unani** (Greco-Arabic): based on the **four humours** (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile), developed through Ibn Sina's *Canon of Medicine*.
- **Oral Indigenous traditions** in Africa, the Americas and Oceania, passed on by healers rather than texts.

**Drugs that trace back to traditional use:**
- **Reserpine** from *Rauvolfia serpentina* (Ayurvedic *sarpagandha*, used for agitation and snakebite), isolated at Ciba in 1952 and used against high blood pressure.
- **Ephedrine** from *ma huang* (*Ephedra sinica*), a TCM remedy for wheezing. Nagai Nagayoshi isolated it in 1885; K. K. Chen and Carl Schmidt described its pharmacology in 1924.
- **Tubocurarine** from Amazonian curare.
- **Galantamine**, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor for Alzheimer disease, from snowdrops (*Galanthus*), which had folk uses in Eastern Europe.
- **Quinine** from cinchona bark, used in the Andes before reaching Europe.

**Ethics and law.** The 1992 **Convention on Biological Diversity** declared that nations have sovereign rights over their genetic resources. The **Nagoya Protocol** (adopted 2010, in force 2014) requires prior informed consent and fair **access and benefit-sharing** with source countries and communities.

Traditional use is a lead, not proof. Plenty of traditional remedies show no benefit in controlled trials, and some are toxic.
levels.phd:
The quantitative case for ethnobotanical drug discovery rests largely on **Fabricant and Farnsworth (2001)**. They identified 122 compounds of defined structure, from 94 plant species, used as drugs worldwide, and found that about 80% were used for the same or a related purpose as the plant's traditional ethnomedical use. This suggests that traditional knowledge carries real pharmacological signal.

Whether that signal beats random screening is debated. Ethnobotanical selection can raise hit rates for specific indications such as anti-infectives or anti-inflammatories. Critics note that high-throughput screening against molecular targets works poorly with traditional categories like 'fever' or 'weakness', which map onto many mechanisms. They also argue that published successes suffer from survivorship bias.

**Quantitative ethnobotany** tries to make field data testable:
- **Informant consensus factor** (Trotter and Logan, 1986): agreement among independent informants on plants for a given ailment category. High consensus suggests a use is not idiosyncratic.
- **Fidelity level** (Friedman et al., 1986): the share of informants citing a plant for one particular use.
- **Use value**: how many uses informants report for a species.

Mechanistic coherence can be striking. Reserpine irreversibly inhibits the **vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT)**, depleting stored noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin. That explains both its traditional calming use and its antihypertensive action, and also the depression it can cause. Tubocurarine is a competitive antagonist at **nicotinic acetylcholine receptors** of the neuromuscular junction, matching curare's paralysing effect.

A classic modern case is **prostratin**, a phorbol ester from *Homalanthus nutans*, a Samoan remedy for hepatitis recorded by Paul Alan Cox. It activates protein kinase C and was studied for reactivating latent HIV reservoirs. The Samoan village of Falealupo negotiated a share of any proceeds, an early benefit-sharing model.

Biopiracy disputes shaped current law. A US patent on turmeric for wound healing was revoked in 1997 after India's CSIR showed prior art in ancient texts. A European patent on a neem-derived fungicide was revoked after opposition, a decision upheld in 2005. These cases drove the creation of India's **Traditional Knowledge Digital Library** to document prior art.
levels.expert:
For clinician-scientists, traditional medicine is both a source of leads and a source of real patient exposures.

**Translational record.** Very few ethnobotany-led programmes reach approval. Shaman Pharmaceuticals, founded in 1989 to build an entire pipeline from healer interviews, failed commercially. Yet its lead, **crofelemer**, a proanthocyanidin oligomer from the latex of *Croton lechleri* (*sangre de drago*, used in Amazonian practice for diarrhoea), was approved by the FDA in 2012 for HIV-associated diarrhoea. It inhibits intestinal chloride secretion through CFTR and calcium-activated chloride channels. It was the first oral botanical drug approved under FDA botanical guidance, which accepts a characterized mixture rather than a single molecule.

**Benefit-sharing in practice.** South Africa's CSIR patented **P57**, an appetite-suppressant compound from *Hoodia gordonii*, a plant the San peoples used to stave off hunger. After protest, a 2003 agreement promised the San royalties. The licensees later abandoned development, so little money flowed. The case shows that consent and contracts matter, but they cannot create value if the product fails.

**Safety pitfalls you will see clinically:**
- **Misidentification and substitution.** In 1990s Belgium, a slimming regimen in which *Aristolochia fangchi* replaced *Stephania tetrandra* (the Chinese names are similar) caused progressive kidney failure and later urothelial cancers. This became known as **aristolochic acid nephropathy**. Aristolochic acids form DNA adducts and leave a characteristic A:T to T:A mutational signature now detected in tumours across Asia.
- **Contamination.** Saper and colleagues (JAMA, 2004) found lead, mercury or arsenic in about one in five Ayurvedic products bought in Boston. Some *rasa shastra* preparations include metals on purpose.
- **Herb-drug interactions** and undisclosed use. Always ask about it directly.

**Institutional shifts.** **ICD-11** added a supplementary chapter on traditional medicine conditions, drawn mainly from Chinese, Japanese and Korean practice. The WHO opened its **Global Centre for Traditional Medicine** in Jamnagar, India, in 2022.

**Open questions:** how to run rigorous trials of individualized multi-herb formulas, how to protect knowledge that exists only orally, and how digital sequence information fits within Nagoya-style benefit-sharing.

lessons.title: Sertürner Isolates Morphine: The Birth of Alkaloid Chemistry

levels.kid:
Long ago, people used a sticky juice from the poppy flower, called **opium**, to ease pain. But there was a problem. Some batches were weak and some were very strong, so doctors could not be sure what they were giving.

Around 1804, a young German pharmacy helper named **Friedrich Sertürner** had an idea. Maybe one special ingredient hidden in the juice was doing the work. He used careful chemistry to pull it out as tiny white crystals.

He named it **morphine**, after **Morpheus**, the Greek god of dreams, because it made people sleepy.

Now doctors could know exactly how strong their medicine was. Morphine still helps people with very bad pain today. Because it is so powerful, doctors decide carefully when to use it.
levels.hs:
**Opium** is the dried milky sap (latex) from the unripe seed pods of the opium poppy, *Papaver somniferum*. For thousands of years it was used for pain, cough and diarrhea. But opium is a **crude drug**: a natural mixture whose strength varies from batch to batch.

In about 1804, **Friedrich Wilhelm Sertürner**, a 21-year-old apothecary's assistant in Paderborn, Germany, asked a bold question: is one single substance responsible for opium's effects? He dissolved opium in acid, then added **ammonia**, a base. Crystals formed. He called this substance the 'sleep-making principle' and later **morphium**, after Morpheus, the god of dreams. The French chemist Gay-Lussac turned the name into **morphine**.

Why was this a big deal?
- It was the first **active ingredient** ever purified from a plant.
- Morphine behaved like a **base**: it reacted with acids to form **salts**. Nobody expected plants to make bases.
- In 1819 the pharmacist Wilhelm Meissner named these plant bases **alkaloids**, meaning 'alkali-like'. Alkaloids are nitrogen-containing compounds, and many are powerful drugs or poisons.

Today we know morphine relieves pain by activating **mu-opioid receptors** on nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. A real example of the change Sertürner started: doctors could now give a known, consistent amount of a pure compound instead of guessing with raw opium.
levels.college:
**Background.** Opium contains roughly two dozen alkaloids. Morphine typically makes up around 10% of its weight, alongside codeine, thebaine, papaverine and noscapine. Before 1800, chemists assumed plant activity came from acids, oils or a vague 'essence', not from a single defined molecule.

**The isolation.** In 1803 the French pharmacist Charles Derosne obtained a crystalline 'opium salt' (probably mostly what we now call noscapine) but did not grasp its basic nature. Sertürner, working in Paderborn from about 1804, published his first results in 1805-1806 and his decisive paper in 1817: 'On morphium, a new salt-forming base, and meconic acid, as main constituents of opium.' Key steps:
- Opium extracted with water and acid, so morphine dissolves as a salt (in opium it occurs bound to **meconic acid**).
- **Ammonia** added to neutralize the solution, causing the free base to crystallize.
- He showed the crystals neutralized acids and formed salts, like mineral alkalis.
- He tested the substance on himself and young volunteers, recording sedation and toxicity, a risky early form of human pharmacology.

**The cascade.** Sertürner's 1817 paper triggered a rush. Within a few years chemists isolated:
- **Emetine** (Pelletier and Magendie, 1817), **strychnine** (1818) and **quinine** from cinchona bark (1820) by Pierre-Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Caventou
- **Caffeine** (Runge, 1819) and **codeine** from opium (Robiquet, 1832)

Meissner's term **alkaloid** (1819) gave the class its name.

**Industry and medicine.** In 1827 Heinrich Emanuel **Merck** in Darmstadt began making morphine commercially, a founding moment of the pharmaceutical industry. Alexander Wood's hypodermic syringe (1853) allowed injection, which made analgesia more reliable but also contributed to dependence.

**Structure.** Morphine's complex structure took over a century to solve: Robert Robinson proposed it in 1925, and Marshall **Gates** completed the first total synthesis in 1952. The mu-opioid receptor itself was only demonstrated in 1973.
levels.phd:
**Acid-base logic of the isolation.** Morphine (C17H19NO3) is amphoteric: a tertiary amine (conjugate acid pKa about 8.2) and a phenolic 3-OH (pKa about 9.9). In acidic water it exists as a soluble ammonium salt. Mild base such as ammonia brings the pH near the isoelectric region, where the neutral species is least water-soluble and crystallizes. Excess strong base (NaOH) ionizes the phenol and redissolves morphine as a phenolate, so the choice of ammonia was chemically fortunate. That same phenolic behaviour was later exploited to separate morphine from non-phenolic co-alkaloids such as codeine and thebaine.

**Priority.** Derosne (1803) and Armand Seguin (reported 1804, published 1814) also obtained crystalline opium fractions. Historians credit Sertürner because he identified a single basic compound, linked it to pharmacological activity, and defined a new chemical category. His early papers were largely ignored until the 1817 publication and Gay-Lussac's endorsement.

**Structure elucidation.** Morphine is a pentacyclic **morphinan** with five stereocenters and a 4,5-epoxy bridge. Degradation chemistry produced the Gulland-Robinson structure (1925); Gates' synthesis (1952) confirmed it, and X-ray crystallography by Mackay and Dorothy Hodgkin (1955) settled the stereochemistry.

**Biosynthesis.** In the poppy, two L-tyrosine units yield (S)-norcoclaurine, then (S)-reticuline, the branch point of benzylisoquinoline alkaloid metabolism. Morphine requires epimerization to (R)-reticuline by **STORR**, a fused P450-oxidoreductase enzyme reported in 2015. Salutaridine synthase (CYP719B1) forms the C-C phenol coupling, leading to **thebaine**. Facchini's group (2010) identified the 2-oxoglutarate-dependent demethylases T6ODM and CODM that convert thebaine via codeine to morphine. In 2015 Smolke's lab engineered yeast with more than 20 heterologous enzymes to make thebaine and hydrocodone from sugar.

**Receptor pharmacology.** Pert and Snyder, Simon, and Terenius independently demonstrated stereospecific opioid binding sites in 1973. Hughes and Kosterlitz identified the enkephalins in 1975, showing that morphine mimics endogenous peptides. Morphine is a mu-opioid receptor (MOR) agonist; MOR couples to Gi/o, inhibiting adenylyl cyclase, opening GIRK channels and closing voltage-gated calcium channels to reduce nociceptive transmission.
levels.expert:
Sertürner's lasting contribution was conceptual: a pure compound makes **dose-response pharmacology** possible. Every modern principle of opioid therapy, from titration to receptor occupancy, rests on that shift. Clinically, morphine remains the WHO reference opioid and an essential medicine, yet the Lancet Commission on palliative care (2017) documented vast global inequity in access, while high-income countries faced an overdose epidemic.

**Metabolism pitfalls.**
- Morphine is glucuronidated mainly by **UGT2B7** to morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G), which lacks analgesic activity and is linked to neuroexcitation, and morphine-6-glucuronide (**M6G**), an active MOR agonist.
- Both glucuronides are renally cleared. In kidney failure, M6G accumulation can produce delayed, prolonged sedation and respiratory depression.
- **Codeine** is a prodrug O-demethylated by **CYP2D6** to morphine. Ultrarapid metabolizers make more morphine, more quickly; pediatric deaths after tonsillectomy led the FDA to a 2013 boxed warning and a 2017 contraindication in children under 12.

**Neurosurgical relevance.**
- Opioid-induced **miosis** can mask a dilating pupil, a key sign of herniation.
- Respiratory depression, mediated largely by MOR in the preBötzinger complex and other brainstem sites, raises PaCO2, causing cerebral vasodilation and higher intracranial pressure in a patient with poor compliance.
- Sedation confounds the serial neurological exam after craniotomy, so analgesic strategies are usually multimodal.
- **Naloxone**, a competitive MOR antagonist, reverses effects but can unmask severe pain and sympathetic surges.

**Open questions.** The **biased agonism** hypothesis held that analgesia flows through G-protein signaling while respiratory depression depends on beta-arrestin-2, based on knockout mouse data (Bohn and colleagues, 1999-2000). It motivated oliceridine (FDA-approved 2020). However, Kliewer and colleagues (2019-2020) found that mice with phosphorylation-deficient MOR, which recruit beta-arrestin poorly, still developed respiratory depression, and later analyses suggested that apparent bias often reflects low intrinsic efficacy. Separating analgesia from respiratory risk at the receptor level remains unresolved.

Other frontiers include microbial biosynthesis of opiates (raising both supply and regulatory questions) and structure-guided design using cryo-EM structures of MOR bound to agonists.

lessons.title: From Willow Bark to Aspirin: Salicin to Acetylsalicylic Acid

levels.kid:
Long, long ago, people noticed something special about willow trees. If you had a fever or achy joints, you could chew a little of the bark or drink a bitter tea made from it. Then you would feel a bit better.

Much later, scientists found the helper hiding inside the bark. They named it **salicin**, after *Salix*, the willow's science name. Your body turns salicin into **salicylic acid**, which fights pain and fever.

But there was a problem. Pure salicylic acid upset people's tummies and tasted awful. So chemists gave it a tiny chemical 'coat.' That new, gentler medicine was called **aspirin**.

So a famous medicine in many family cupboards started its story as a tree growing beside a river!
levels.hs:
Willow trees (genus **Salix**) have been used against pain and fever for thousands of years. Ancient Sumerian and Egyptian texts mention willow, and Greek physicians recommended it too.

The modern story starts in 1763. That year an English clergyman, the **Reverend Edward Stone**, reported to the Royal Society that powdered willow bark had cured 'agues' (fevers) in about 50 patients over several years.

Chemists then hunted for the active ingredient:
- **1828–1829**: Johann Buchner in Germany and Henri Leroux in France isolated **salicin**, a bitter crystalline compound from willow bark.
- **1838**: Raffaele Piria converted salicin into **salicylic acid**, the compound that does most of the work in the body.
- **1859**: Hermann Kolbe made salicylic acid from phenol, so it no longer had to come from trees.

Salicylic acid relieved fever and joint pain. However, it badly irritated the stomach and tasted terrible. In 1897 **Felix Hoffmann**, a chemist at the German company **Bayer**, attached an **acetyl group** to it. An acetyl group is a small chemical piece related to acetic acid, the acid in vinegar. The result, **acetylsalicylic acid (ASA)**, was gentler and more stable. Bayer named it **Aspirin** in 1899.

Aspirin works by blocking an enzyme called **cyclooxygenase (COX)**. COX makes **prostaglandins**, chemical signals that cause pain, fever and inflammation.
levels.college:
**From crude drug to pure molecule.** Willow bark shows pharmacognosy's classic arc: first a traditional crude drug, then an isolated natural product, then a semisynthetic improvement.

- **Salicin** is a **glucoside**: a glucose sugar joined to an aromatic alcohol called **saligenin** (salicyl alcohol). On its own it is largely inactive, so it acts as a natural **prodrug**.
- After salicin is swallowed, gut bacteria and enzymes split off the glucose. Saligenin is absorbed, and the liver oxidizes it to **salicylic acid** (2-hydroxybenzoic acid).

**A second plant source.** In 1835 Karl Löwig obtained 'spiric acid' from **meadowsweet**, then called *Spiraea ulmaria*. It proved identical to salicylic acid, and that plant gave aspirin its name: **a-** (acetyl) + **spir** (Spiraea) + **-in**.

**Industrial chemistry takes over.** Kolbe's 1859 synthesis from phenol and carbon dioxide, later improved by Rudolf Schmitt as the **Kolbe–Schmitt reaction**, made salicylic acid cheap. From the 1870s it was used for rheumatic fever, gout and fever. Its drawbacks were stomach irritation, nausea and a foul taste.

**Acetylation.** Charles Gerhardt first made acetylsalicylic acid in 1853, but his product was impure and unstable, and he did not pursue it. On 10 August 1897 Felix Hoffmann at Bayer made pure, stable ASA by reacting salicylic acid with **acetic anhydride**. Bayer's pharmacologist **Heinrich Dreser** was initially skeptical, but trials followed, and the Aspirin trademark was registered in March 1899.

**Mechanism.** In 1971 **John Vane** showed that aspirin-like drugs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, work recognized by the 1982 Nobel Prize. Aspirin transfers its acetyl group onto a **serine** in the COX active site, blocking the enzyme **irreversibly**. COX makes two kinds of products:
- prostaglandins, which drive pain, fever and inflammation
- **thromboxane A2**, which makes platelets clump

**Platelets** have no nucleus, so they cannot make new COX. One exposure therefore blocks a platelet for its whole lifespan, about 7–10 days. This is why aspirin is used to help prevent heart attacks and strokes.
levels.phd:
**Chemistry of the series.** Salicin is the β-D-glucopyranoside of saligenin (2-hydroxybenzyl alcohol). Piria (1838) hydrolysed it to glucose and saligenin, then oxidized saligenin via salicylaldehyde to salicylic acid. Acetylation targets the phenolic hydroxyl, giving 2-acetoxybenzoic acid. Gerhardt treated sodium salicylate with acetyl chloride. Hoffmann used acetic anhydride and obtained a product stable enough to formulate. In the Kolbe–Schmitt reaction, sodium phenoxide is carboxylated by CO2 under heat and pressure, with ortho selectivity.

**Biosynthesis in plants.** Salicylic acid is a plant defense hormone that governs **systemic acquired resistance**. Arabidopsis makes most of its pathogen-induced SA from chorismate via **isochorismate synthase (ICS1)**, and a PAL-dependent phenylpropanoid route also contributes. Salicin and related salicinoids in *Salix* and *Populus* defend against herbivores. Recent poplar work implicates benzoyl-CoA-derived benzoate esters and specific UDP-glycosyltransferases (such as UGT71L1), but the pathway is not fully resolved.

**Pharmacology.** Plasma and liver esterases hydrolyse ASA's ester rapidly, with a half-life of roughly 15–20 minutes. Platelets passing through the portal circulation are therefore acetylated before much systemic ASA exists. Roth and Majerus (1975) used radiolabelled acetyl groups to show covalent acetylation of a platelet protein. The site was later mapped to **Ser530** of COX-1 (Ser516 in COX-2). The bound acetyl group sterically blocks arachidonate from reaching the catalytic **Tyr385** radical. Acetylated COX-2 still has activity: it switches to forming 15(R)-HETE, which leukocyte 5-lipoxygenase converts to **aspirin-triggered lipoxins** (Serhan), which are pro-resolving mediators.

**The salicylate paradox.** In vitro, salicylate is a weak, reversible COX inhibitor, yet it is anti-inflammatory at high plasma concentrations. Proposed explanations include:
- inhibition of **IKKβ/NF-κB** signalling (Kopp and Ghosh, 1994; Yin et al., 1998)
- direct activation of **AMPK** (Hawley et al., 2012)
- suppression of COX-2 gene expression

How much each contributes clinically is still debated.

**Priority dispute.** In 1949 Arthur Eichengrün claimed he had directed Hoffmann's work. Walter Sneader's 2000 reanalysis supported this claim, noting that the story of Hoffmann's father's rheumatism first appeared in a 1934 account. Bayer rejects this reading.
levels.expert:
**Clinical legacy.** Aspirin's main modern role is as an antiplatelet drug. ISIS-2 (1988) showed that aspirin reduced vascular death after myocardial infarction, with benefit additive to streptokinase. Secondary prevention after MI or ischaemic stroke is now well established. Primary prevention is a different story. In 2018, ASPREE (healthy older adults), ARRIVE (moderate-risk adults) and ASCEND (diabetes) found small or absent vascular gains, largely offset by major bleeding. Guidelines have since moved away from routine use in people without vascular disease.

**Pitfalls:**
- **NSAID interaction**: ibuprofen reversibly fills the COX-1 channel. Taken before aspirin, it shields Ser530 from acetylation and blunts the antiplatelet effect (FDA communication, 2006).
- **Reye syndrome**: its link with salicylates in children with influenza or varicella led to warnings in the 1980s, after which cases fell sharply.
- **Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease** (Samter's triad): asthma, nasal polyps and reactions to COX-1 inhibitors, attributed to arachidonate shunting toward cysteinyl leukotrienes.
- **Salicylate toxicity**: tinnitus, respiratory alkalosis from direct stimulation of the respiratory centre, then metabolic acidosis as oxidative phosphorylation is uncoupled.
- **Neurosurgery**: platelet inhibition persists until platelets are replaced. Surgeons must weigh the thrombotic risk of stopping aspirin against bleeding inside the rigid skull. In the PATCH trial (2016), platelet transfusion for antiplatelet-associated spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage worsened outcomes.

**Open questions.** 'Aspirin resistance' may largely reflect nonadherence, poor absorption from enteric-coated tablets or high platelet turnover. Rothwell's meta-analyses and the CAPP2 trial in Lynch syndrome suggest fewer colorectal cancers, possibly through platelet-mediated mechanisms. Aspirin started early in high-risk pregnancies reduced preterm preeclampsia (ASPRE, 2017).

**Back to the bark.** Willow bark extracts standardized to salicin are still sold. They act slowly and have weaker antiplatelet effects, because their product, salicylate, lacks the acetyl group needed for irreversible COX block. They also contain other polyphenols, and content varies between products. After World War I, reparations and a 1921 US court ruling turned 'aspirin' into a generic word in several countries, though it remains a Bayer trademark in many others.

test.q: Chemically, salicin from willow bark is best described as:
test.explain: Salicin is a glucoside: glucose joined to saligenin. It contains no nitrogen, so it is not an alkaloid like morphine.

test.q: What was the main problem with salicylic acid as a medicine in the 1870s–1890s?
choices: It cost too much to produce
test.explain: Salicylic acid worked against fever and joint pain, but it irritated the stomach and tasted foul. Kolbe's synthesis had already made it cheap.

test.q: What did Felix Hoffmann achieve at Bayer in 1897?
test.explain: Hoffmann acetylated salicylic acid with acetic anhydride to make pure, stable acetylsalicylic acid. Salicin was isolated around 1828–1829, and Kolbe synthesized salicylic acid from phenol.

test.q: The 'spir' in the name Aspirin refers to:
test.explain: Meadowsweet was then called Spiraea ulmaria and was a source of salicylic acid. A- stands for acetyl, and -in was a common drug-name ending.

test.q: How does aspirin inactivate cyclooxygenase (COX)?
choices: It competes reversibly for the site
It switches off the enzyme's gene
test.explain: Aspirin transfers its acetyl group onto a serine in COX's active site, blocking the enzyme irreversibly. Reversible competition describes drugs like ibuprofen.

test.q: Why does aspirin's effect on platelets last for the platelet's whole lifespan?
choices: Aspirin stays in the blood for weeks
The liver releases aspirin very slowly
Platelets store aspirin in their granules
Platelets have no nucleus for new COX
test.explain: Without a nucleus, platelets cannot make new COX, so the block lasts until they are replaced in about 7–10 days. Aspirin itself is cleared from the blood quickly.

test.q: Whose 1971 work showed that aspirin-like drugs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis?
test.explain: John Vane identified the mechanism and shared the 1982 Nobel Prize. Gerhardt first made impure ASA in 1853, and Dreser was Bayer's pharmacologist.

test.q: Hermann Kolbe's 1859 contribution to the salicylate story was that he:
choices: Named the new drug for Bayer
test.explain: Kolbe synthesized salicylic acid from phenol and carbon dioxide, later improved as the Kolbe–Schmitt reaction. This freed production from plant sources.

test.q: What is the Latin genus name of willow trees, which gave salicin its name?
test.explain: Salicin, salicylic acid and salicylates are all named after Salix, the willow genus.

test.q: In the body, salicin is converted into ___ acid, the compound that does most of the work.
test.explain: Salicin is a prodrug. The glucose is removed, and the liver oxidizes saligenin to salicylic acid.

test.q: Aspirin blocks the enzyme ___, which makes prostaglandins and thromboxane.
test.explain: Cyclooxygenase (COX) converts arachidonic acid into prostaglandins and thromboxane A2.

Its product, salicylate, lacks the acetyl group for lasting COX block
It binds albumin so tightly that little reaches platelets

advancedTest.q: Ibuprofen taken shortly before aspirin can blunt aspirin's cardioprotective effect. What best explains this?

It induces fresh COX-1 synthesis in mature platelets
It reversibly fills the COX-1 channel, shielding Ser530
It blocks thromboxane receptors, hiding aspirin's effect

It acetylates COX-2 in inflamed tissue
It is re-acetylated to aspirin in the liver
